To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the brain of diapausing pupae of a butterfly is arrested at an early stage, 2) sensory structures related to visual information processing are well developed in diapausing pupal brains, 3) the brain develops further only after diapause, when temperatures increase, and 4) the brain of direct developing pupae is well developed at the same time when it is arrested in diapausing ones.

(i) the brain grows in size during both diapause and direct development, (ii) the development of the visual system is arrested in diapause but not in direct development, and (iii) the development of olfactory system is arrested in both diapause pupae and in direct pupae, and only continues in the latter.

(i) brain development is arrested in pupae of a butterfly species during diapause; and (ii) visual neuropils are well developed in both diapause and direct pupae, whereas olfactory neuropils only develop in direct pupae.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how neural development during diapausing development is affected by conflicting selective pressures.
the development of the brain during diapause in a butterfly.
the development and maintenance of the brain during diapause as a possible mechanism to explain diapause duration in insects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

sensory structures related to visual perception are well developed in both pathways of diapause development, while sensory structures related to olfaction are well developed in non-diapause development only.
the development of the visual system is important for diapause development, while the olfactory system is important for normal post-diapause development.
the brain is not a cost-free organ and that there might be trade-offs between the need for neural structures to be developed during the pupal stage and the need to save energy during diapause.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
diapause is not a period of neural development arrest but rather of arrested development in certain parts of the brain.
the brain develops idiosyncratically during diapause.

sensory structures in the diapausing brain develop in a highly idiosyncratic fashion, and that the development of sensory structures is more closely related to the diapause pathway than the overall brain size.
The main takeaway from our work is that
neural development in diapause pupae is idiosyncratic and not simply a scaled down version of development in direct pupae, with implications for the information processing capacity of the brain.
diapause is a time of idiosyncratic neural development, and that the brain is not a passive structure during diapause.
the development of neural structures during diapause is not simply an extrapolation of development during non-diapause.
